newsitem.title: USA: Consumer prices muted in June, output rises steadily.
newsitem.headline: Consumer prices muted in June, output rises steadily.

text.p: Consumer prices barely rose in June while industrial output grew steadily with no sign of strain, economic reports showed Wednesday, keeping inflation at its lowest level in a decade.
The reports helped sparked a rally on Wall Street as investors bet the Federal Reserve would see little pressure to raise interest rates soon to ward off inflation.

The Labour Department said the Consumer Price Index rose a scant 0.1 percent in June, the fourth consecutive 0.1 percent increase. The so-called core rate, excluding volatile food and energy costs, also rose just 0.1 percent, the slowest pace for the first half of the year in 32 years.

Separately, the Federal Reserve said industrial production increased 0.3 percent in June after a revised 0.2 percent rise in May. Together the reports painted a picture of a strong economy with remarkably little inflation after more than six years of growth.
Businesses ran at 83.5 percent of capacity last month, indicating little difficulty for them to boost output using their existing plants, factories and work forces.

"I think what this is telling us is that there's almost a complete lack of inflationary pressures in the economy," Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc., said on Reuters Financial Television.
Investors celebrated after the reports, driving stock prices higher and long-term interest rates lower.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 41.80 points to 8,017.51 at midday and the 30-year Treasury bond jumped almost a full point, lowering its yield to 6.48 percent from 6.55 percent on Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Analysts said the reports offered fresh hope that Fed policy-makers will hold short-term rates steady for some time.

Economist Josh Feinman of Bankers Trust Co. in New York said the industrial output report confirmed that manufacturers could boost output without much strain and hence there was no need for higher rates.
"There is nothing in here to get in the way of the market feeling that the Federal Reserve is on hold and the good times can continue," Feinman said.

The Fed held short-term rates steady at its last two meetings in May and earlier this month after raising them in March, the first increase in more than two years. Fed policy-makers are next set to meet on Aug. 19.
In its report Wednesday, the Fed said automakers raised assembly rates in June, boosting overall output, as did high-technology industries.
The Labour Department said consumer prices rose at a 1.4 percent annual rate in the first six months of 1997, less than half the 3.3 percent rise for all of 1996.
Lower energy costs and modestly higher food prices helped keep the index's overall rise in the first half to the smallest since 1986, the department said.
A separate Commerce Department report showed a modest rise in business inventories in May as sales fell at the sharpest rate in nearly a year.

Stocks of unsold goods rose 0.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted $1.02 trillion after a revised 0.4 percent gain in April, the department said. Sales fell 0.5 percent in May after a 0.2 percent pickup in April.

Department officials said it was the largest drop in monthly sales since a 0.7 percent fall in June 1996, a sign that consumers spent less in the second quarter, further reducing potential price pressures.
